title: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)
summary: The Windows logon script sub-technique uses the per-user registry value that names a program to run each time that user signs in. Because the value belongs to the signed-in user and runs in the user's session, writing it needs only the rights of that account, which makes it a practical persistence option for an adversary who already controls a normal user. The referenced program can be a script interpreter, a command file or an executable, and the path often points to a user profile or temporary directory rather than to a managed script share, which is itself a useful indicator. Detection compares the registry value against the scripts the organisation deploys through policy, then correlates logon events with the execution of the referenced file and with any network activity that follows. Legitimate software and administrators do use logon scripts, especially in older domain designs, so the strongest signals are the value being created or changed outside a change window, a path inconsistent with the policy convention, and a script that is new, unsigned and rarely seen in the environment.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker sets a Windows program to run every time a chosen user signs in. It uses a per-user setting in the registry. The registry is a store of system and user settings. The setting names a file to run, and Windows runs it at sign in.
beginner.whyItMatters: This setting needs only the rights of a normal user account. An attacker who has any user account can add it. The program then returns every time that user signs in. There is no need to stay connected or to keep a service running. It is quiet persistence that survives restarts.
howItWorks: The attacker gets control of a normal user account on the machine.
They place their script or program somewhere the account can write, often in the user profile.
They change the per-user logon script value in the registry to point at that file.
The next time the user signs in, Windows runs the named program automatically.
The program runs in the user session and can contact the attacker or start more tools.
The registry value stays in place, so the program returns at every later sign in.
beginner.example: Imagine a flat where each person leaves a note for the cleaner on their own door. One tenant writes please water the plants. The cleaner waters them every visit. The landlord never sees the note, because it is on the tenant's own door.
takeaways: Per-user settings can give persistence without administrator rights.
Registry values that name startup programs should be baselined.
A logon script path inside a user profile is a strong warning sign.

objectives: Identify the registry setting used for per-user Windows logon scripts.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent technique.
Explain why a normal user account is enough to create this persistence.
Describe the artefacts that show a logon script was added or changed.
Correlate logon events with the script that ran afterwards.
